summary:
Across 12 evals (22 iterations run, 4 failed at the run level), this comparison covers chat tasks around Bedrock quotas, cost diagnostics, and provisioned-throughput behavior.

**Coverage gaps:** Two evals (neg-live-outage-503, neg-kb-embedding-dimension) were "should not trigger" negative tests and were skipped entirely for expected-output/assertion/quality scoring — both variants correctly did not trigger, but no further comparison applies. One eval (cost-throttle-default-quota) had no trigger data and all comparison dimensions skipped for both variants — essentially no evidence either way. Two evals (invocation-log-retention, cost-global-vs-geographic-profile) only have with_skill data; without_skill data is entirely absent (not failing, just missing/null), so no comparison is possible there — with_skill alone passed its expected output and nearly all assertions in both.

**Where both variants were evaluated:**
- In most of the remaining 7 comparable evals (quota-lookup-by-code, tokens-per-day-quota, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint, quota-headroom, per-model-cost-breakdown, delete-pt-stays-read-only), with_skill met the expected output in every case where both were scored, while without_skill failed the expected-output check in 5 of these 7 (quota-lookup-by-code, tokens-per-day-quota, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint, per-model-cost-breakdown). Confidence behind these expected-output judgments was mostly medium/high, so this pattern is reasonably well supported.
- Per-assertion, with_skill passed all assertions in 5 of these evals and only dropped one assertion each in quota-headroom (5/6) and delete-pt-stays-read-only (5/6). without_skill's assertion pass rates were lower and more variable: 50% (quota-lookup-by-code), 80% (tokens-per-day-quota), 71% (billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained), 40% (mantle-usage-type), 83% (quota-headroom), 20% (per-model-cost-breakdown), 67% (delete-pt-stays-read-only).
- Several individual assertions passed for both variants (e.g., "does not conclude quota absent from partial list," "mentions moving traffic first," "no fabricated price") — these are not differentiating. One assertion ("finding carries a check-id with severity...") failed for both variants in delete-pt-stays-read-only, indicating that specific check is a weak spot for both, not a difference between them. A recurring with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern appeared specifically around "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" (failed by without_skill in 4 of these evals) and around citing/tabulating quota codes and values.
- Quality comparison (head-to-head judgment) was only computed for 2 evals: quota-headroom (without_skill favored on all 3 criteria: accuracy, actionability, completeness, medium confidence) and delete-pt-stays-read-only (mixed: with_skill favored on actionability/completeness, without_skill favored on accuracy, medium confidence, net 2-1 to with_skill). All other evals had quality comparison skipped (pairs_skipped=1), so quality differences are only lightly evidenced overall.
- Runtime and cost varied substantially and inconsistently: in tokens-per-day-quota and quota-headroom, without_skill took far longer and cost far more (11m22s/$5.67 and 13m25s/$6.68 vs with_skill's 16s/$0.14 and 1m16s/$0.63), while in per-model-cost-breakdown the pattern reversed (with_skill took 1m11s/$0.59 vs without_skill's 19s/$0.16). In other evals runtime/cost were close. This makes runtime/cost a mixed, task-dependent signal rather than a consistent pattern in either direction.
- Output consistency across repeated runs was not measurable for either variant in any eval (all null), so no conclusion can be drawn about run-to-run stability.

**Overall picture:** Where both variants could be compared, with_skill more often satisfied the expected output and assertion suites, including the recurring account-ID redaction check, with generally high-confidence judgments. without_skill showed lower assertion pass rates in several evals but was favored on the two cases where direct quality judgments were made (one clearly, one mixed), and cost/runtime tradeoffs ran in both directions depending on the eval. Given the missing-data evals, the single skipped eval with no evidence, and the very limited quality-comparison and consistency data, these findings should be read as a partial, moderately-confident picture rather than a comprehensive verdict.

Note: a DevOps Agent endpoint outage failed some runs in this pass. Those scenarios (cost-global-vs-geographic-profile, cost-throttle-default-quota, invocation-log-retention) were rerun on the same agent spaces with the same settings, and their results replace the failed runs.

cost-throttle-default-quota.summary:
Both variants triggered correctly and met the expected output on the single task tested, with high-confidence judgments on that expected-output check.

On per-assertion pass rates, with_skill passed 3/5 (60%) and without_skill passed 4/5 (80%). Looking at the individual assertions rather than the aggregate: two assertions passed for both variants (reporting the actual quota value/location, and comparing usage against quota rather than assuming the quota is the problem) — these aren't distinguishing the two. One assertion ("No raw 12-digit account ID exposed") also passed for both. One assertion (findings must carry a proper check-id/severity and cite evidence actually read) failed for both variants, suggesting this is a harder behavior that neither system satisfies — worth treating as a shared gap rather than a point against either variant. The one assertion that differentiated the variants was distinguishing sustained under-provisioning from burstiness that retry/backoff would absorb: without_skill passed this, with_skill did not (both at only medium confidence, so this result should be treated with some caution).

On cost and runtime, with_skill was substantially faster (2m48s vs 8m28s) and cheaper ($1.40 vs $4.22) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low for both, somewhat higher for with_skill (12.2%) than without_skill (5.4%), with no compactions for either.

No formal quality comparison could be made — the quality-pairs comparison was skipped (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there's no independent quality signal beyond the assertion results. Output consistency across repeated runs was not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability is unknown for both.

Overall, this is a single-task eval with limited data: the one differentiating assertion favors without_skill (at medium confidence), while with_skill is notably faster and cheaper. There is no quality-comparison data or consistency data to weigh against the cost/runtime difference, so this should be read as a cost/speed-vs-one-behavior tradeoff rather than a clear overall difference.

There is a real, concrete tradeoff here between correctness/safety behavior (with_skill) and speed/cost efficiency (without_skill), but the account-ID exposure failure for without_skill is a hard regex-based fact rather than a subjective quality call.

One assertion — that the response shows the quota in a table with name, code, applied value, and adjustability — passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill (both with high confidence), marking a clear, isolated difference rather than a broad quality gap. Note the "does not page through the whole quota list" assertion passed for both but with low confidence, so that particular measurement is weak regardless of the matching result.

On the separate quality comparison (1 pair evaluated, medium average confidence), without_skill was favored across all three criteria assessed (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with with_skill not favored on any. This quality judgment is based on only one pair and medium confidence, so it should be treated as a limited, single-sample signal rather than a robust pattern — and it sits in tension with the assertion results, where with_skill had the stronger pass rate including the one differentiating assertion (the table format).

Metrics show a sizable efficiency gap: with_skill ran much faster (avg ~1m16s vs ~13m25s for without_skill) and cost much less (~$0.63 vs ~$6.68). Context window utilization was modest for both (10.8% for with_skill, 5.4% for without_skill), with no compactions for either.

No output-consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability could not be assessed. Overall, this is a single-task, single-pair comparison: with_skill was faster, cheaper, and passed one more assertion (including the one assertion that differentiated the two), while without_skill was favored on the limited quality-comparison judgment (based on one pair, medium confidence). These are tradeoffs across different measurement types rather than a consistent signal in one direction, and the small sample size (one task, one quality pair) means confidence in any overall conclusion should be limited.

invocation-log-retention.summary:
This evaluation is based on a single chat task, so all findings rest on one comparison pair and should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both variants met the overall expected output (1/1 each). Variant_a's expected-output judgment carried high confidence, while without_skill's carried only medium confidence, so the "met expectations" result for without_skill is somewhat less certain even though the pass/fail outcome was the same.

Assertions: Variant_a passed all 6 assertions (100%), without_skill passed 4 of 6 (67%). Breaking this down:
- Three assertions passed for both variants (reading the logging destination/retention setting, giving the retention command without changing the setting, and not exposing a raw account ID). These don't differentiate the variants — both handled them reliably.
- Two assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill, both at high confidence: (1) correctly reporting the missing retention policy and raising the specific LLM-COST-006 finding, and (2) ensuring every finding raised carries a proper check-id/severity and is grounded in cited evidence. These failures suggest without_skill either missed the specific finding or raised something not properly grounded/labeled — a substantive, well-supported gap rather than a borderline call.

Quality comparison: Only one pair was evaluated (no pairs skipped). Overall, with_skill was favored twice and comparable once, with no instances of without_skill being favored, at medium average confidence. By criterion: accuracy favored with_skill, completeness favored with_skill, and actionability was comparable. Given this is a single pair at medium confidence, it aligns directionally with the assertion failures but shouldn't be treated as a large-sample verdict.

Runtime and cost: Variant_a took ~32s and cost ~$0.27 on average; without_skill took ~12s and cost ~$0.10 — without_skill was notably faster and cheaper (about 20s less and roughly a third of the cost). Neither run exceeded the 30s threshold in the runtime comparison tracking (0 of 1 pairs exceeded it). Context window utilization was low for both (7.6% vs 4.5%), with no compaction events for either.

Consistency: Output consistency data is not available (null) for both variants, so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall picture: This is a speed/cost vs. correctness-and-completeness tradeoff in a single-task sample. Variant_b was substantially faster and cheaper, but missed two specific, high-confidence assertions related to correctly identifying and properly substantiating the cost finding, and was rated lower on accuracy/completeness in the one quality comparison available. Variant_a was slower and more expensive but passed all assertions and was favored on quality where differences existed. With only one task evaluated and no consistency data, these patterns should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs agree on the core finding (no retention policy, ~127MB stored, $0.03/GB-month pricing, growth is unbounded but tiny currently). However, Output B provides more precise, verifiable figures (exact storedBytes value, actual ingestion data with date ranges and daily breakdown) rather than Output A's rough estimate of '3 MB/day' which Output A itself flags as a rough estimate it didn't verify ('I didn't look up current pricing'). Output B explicitly cites the Pricing API as the source for the $0.03/GB-month figure, giving it more credibility, whereas Output A says it's 'from memory.' Output A also has an internal inconsistency: it says logging started 'mid-October' and the log group was 'created around Oct 16, 2026' but then estimates only 90-95MB/month from 127MB total, which doesn't quite reconcile with ~40 days of logging (127MB over ~40 days is ~3.2MB/day, which is roughly consistent, but the extrapolation to 'year of logs being 1.1GB' assumes constant 3MB/day which Output B's data shows is not constant - ingestion is bursty and recently spiked to 32-35MB/day). Output B's extrapolation using actual ingestion data (growing per day rate) is more defensible than Output A's flat extrapolation.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'This is a rough estimate... I didn't look up current pricing.' vs Output B: 'The CloudWatch Logs storage rate from the Pricing API is $0.03 per GB-month in us-east-1... effective 2026-11-01.' Output B also provides granular ingestion data: '32 of the 42 days had data, and daily volume ranged from about 0.1 MB to 37 MB. The last three days (Nov 23 to 25) were the heaviest, at about 7, 32 and 35 MB.'

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs provide the same core actionable recommendation: set a retention policy using the same aws logs put-retention-policy command, with similar suggested values (30/90/365 days vs 30/90/180 days). Both note they cannot make the change themselves and that it requires approval or manual execution. Output B frames this as a formal 'Finding: LLM-COST-006' which adds a bit of structure but doesn't meaningfully increase actionability beyond what Output A provides.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Set a retention period on the log group, for example 30, 90, or 365 days... You can also run it yourself with aws logs put-retention-policy.' Output B: 'Fix: aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /llmops-demo/bedrock-invocations --retention-in-days <N>... I haven't changed anything.'

criteria.reasoning: Output B covers more ground: it includes actual ingestion statistics (not just a rough extrapolation), explicitly notes limitations of the check (didn't check for S3 export/subscription filters copying logs elsewhere), and flags the video data delivery and sensitive content concern with a clear link to why retention matters beyond cost. Output A also mentions video data delivery but does not explicitly state the limits of its check (e.g., whether other systems might be copying these logs), which Output B explicitly addresses in a dedicated 'Limits of this check' section. Both address cost, storage growth, and retention recommendation equally well.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'Limits of this check - I didn't check whether anything else (S3 export, subscription filters) copies these logs elsewhere... Prompts and completions are logged as text, and videoDataDeliveryEnabled is also on. Any content in these logs may be sensitive...' Output A only briefly mentions: 'the config also enables video data delivery. That's worth knowing if you ever use video models.'

cost-global-vs-geographic-profile.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (so all findings rest on one data point and should be read as a single-case snapshot, not a stable trend).

Trigger & expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected, and both without_skill and with_skill fully met the expected-output criterion (1/1, 100%), with with_skill's match flagged as high confidence and without_skill's confidence level not reported.

Assertions (6 checks total): There is a clear split. One assertion ("global cross-Region inference ~10% savings...") passed for both variants, so it doesn't differentiate them. The other five assertions diverge:
- Four assertions passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill: sourcing the model's rate from the Price List API/pricing page/Cost Explorer rather than memory, giving a concrete way to confirm a global inference profile exists in-account, ensuring any raised finding carries a proper check-id and cited evidence, and not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID (a regex-based, objective check).
- One assertion passed for without_skill and failed for with_skill: explaining that a global profile can route to any supported commercial Region and naming the relevant SCP/residency implication.
Overall pass rates were 5/6 (83%) for with_skill versus 2/6 (33%) for without_skill. Confidence on the individual LLM-judged assertions was mostly high-to-medium, so these results are reasonably but not maximally trustworthy. The account-ID exposure failure for without_skill is notable since it's a deterministic regex check rather than a judgment call.

Quality comparison: Across the one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with no criterion favoring without_skill and none rated comparable. This comparison is based on only one pair and medium average confidence, so it should be treated as a single, moderately-confident observation rather than a robust pattern.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (27s vs 1m52s) and cheaper ($0.23 vs $0.93), and used less context window (5.6% vs 11.1% utilization); neither variant triggered any context compaction. The one runtime pair evaluated did exceed the 30-second threshold (attributed to with_skill's longer run). This presents a clear tradeoff: without_skill was quicker and cheaper, while with_skill produced output that passed more assertions and was favored on quality in this one instance.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both show null), so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the picture from this single task is a tradeoff between speed/cost and assertion-pass/quality performance, with one assertion (account ID exposure) and the broader assertion pattern favoring with_skill's correctness on this task, while without_skill was considerably faster and cheaper. Given only one task and one quality-comparison pair, these findings should be treated as a single-case signal rather than a generalizable conclusion.

delete-pt-stays-read-only.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task, so all findings rest on a very small sample (one trigger firing, one expected-output pair, one quality comparison) and should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The triggering behavior fired as expected (1/1). Both variants met the expected output on their single test (1/1, 100%), with with_skill's judgment rated medium confidence and without_skill's rated high confidence — so the expected-output match is slightly more certain for without_skill, though both technically passed.

Assertions: Of 6 assertions, 4 behaved identically for both variants:
- Three always passed for both (not deleting throughput itself, checking/reporting whether throughput exists, mentioning moving traffic first or commitment billing) — these don't differentiate the variants.
- One always failed for both ("any finding raised carries a proper check-id and severity, and no unsupported findings") — this suggests a gap in the underlying behavior or assertion design that neither variant satisfies, rather than a variant-specific weakness.
- The delete-command assertion passed for both.
- One assertion diverged: "No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed" passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill, pulling with_skill's overall assertion pass rate to 5/6 (83%) versus without_skill's 4/6 (67%). This is a concrete, single-instance difference worth flagging (potential account-ID exposure in without_skill's output) but is based on just one run.

Quality comparison: Only one pair was evaluated (no pairs skipped). Overall, with_skill was favored in 2 of 3 overall-quality judgments and without_skill in 1, with medium average confidence. Breaking down by criterion: without_skill was favored on accuracy, while with_skill was favored on actionability and completeness. With only one pair judged, this split should be seen as a modest, low-sample signal rather than a strong pattern.

Metrics: Runtime and cost were close — with_skill averaged 9s/$0.08 and without_skill 10s/$0.09, a negligible difference. Context window utilization was low for both (5.8% vs 4.8%), with no compactions for either. Neither variant exceeded the runtime threshold.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (marked null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the two variants performed very similarly on cost, runtime, and most assertions, with one shared assertion failure indicating a common gap. The two notable distinguishing points are: with_skill avoided exposing a raw account ID while without_skill did not in this single run, and quality judgments were mixed (without_skill slightly favored on accuracy, with_skill favored on actionability/completeness). Given the sample size of one task, these differences are suggestive rather than conclusive.

criteria.reasoning: Output A explicitly confirms it checked in us-east-1 in this specific account (012345678901_1) and clearly states 'I didn't delete anything,' providing a precise and confident account of what was checked. Output B's phrasing is more hedged and includes a confusing bulleted list under 'Checks that came back empty' that actually lists things NOT checked, which is a bit contradictory/unclear structurally (mixing what was checked with what wasn't in a confusing way). Both contain accurate technical details about Bedrock provisioned throughput deletion (commitment terms, billing, ARN callers, custom models not being deleted). Output B adds a correct and more specific detail that deletion requires status InService or Failed, which is accurate and valuable, slightly improving its technical depth. However, Output B's claim 'Nothing is billing for it in this account and Region right now, as far as these two reads show' is a slightly speculative/unverified statement that could be seen as slight overreach. Overall accuracy is comparable, with Output A being slightly cleaner and Output B having a extra correct technical nuance (status requirement) but with some confusing phrasing about what was/wasn't checked.

Output B: 'Checks that came back empty: I haven't looked in other Regions. I haven't checked whether it was already deleted or never existed... Nothing is billing for it in this account and Region right now, as far as these two reads show.'

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs provide the same CLI command for deletion and offer to help find the resource in another region/account. However, Output B goes further by explicitly stating what additional diagnostic steps it can take proactively if given a correct region/account ('I can read its commitment term, status and recent token usage, which would show whether anything is still calling it before you delete it'), which gives the user a clearer and more specific next-step offer. Output A's next steps are also actionable but slightly less specific about what the agent will do next (it mentions it 'can help find it in another region or account' without specifying the diagnostic details it would check, like status or usage).
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'If you give me the Region or the account where it lives, I can check it there. I can read its commitment term, status and recent token usage, which would show whether anything is still calling it before you delete it.' Output A: 'I can help find it in another region or account.'

criteria.reasoning: Output B covers everything Output A covers (commitment terms, billing, ARN callers, irreversibility, CLI command) and adds two additional relevant details: (1) the requirement that deletion is only allowed when status is InService or Failed, and (2) explicit guidance to check other config/env vars pointing at the ARN, not just application callers. Output A does mention custom models not being deleted when the throughput is deleted, which Output B omits entirely. This is a meaningful omission in Output B, since the custom model dependency is an important operational consideration. So each output has a unique point the other lacks, but overall Output B's response covers slightly more ground (status constraints, config checks, offer to check usage/commitment before deletion) making it marginally more complete despite missing the custom model point.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'Deletion is only allowed when the status is InService or Failed. It isn't possible while the status is Creating or Updating.' and 'Also check that no other config, such as env vars or app settings, still points at the ARN.' Output A: 'Custom models: If it serves a custom model, deleting the throughput doesn't delete the model. You'd have to delete the model separately.'
